variants.title: Read the promise
variants.context: An accepted intent is durable, no external send bypasses current policy, and retries create at most one logical channel delivery. Accepted means the platform owns the work, not that a provider or device delivered it.
variants.prompt: The API returned accepted for a push notification. What is promised?
options: The platform durably owns the work; delivery to a device is not promised.
optionFeedback: Acceptance is durable ownership.
Device receipt is a later, separate state.
Provider delivery is separate too.

variants.title: Read the promise
variants.context: An accepted intent is durable, no external send bypasses current policy, and retries create at most one logical channel delivery. Accepted means the platform owns the work, not that a provider or device delivered it.
variants.prompt: A worker replays an event and produces a second send to the same recipient channel. Which identity was missing?
options: A stable channel_delivery_id per recipient-channel pair.
optionFeedback: Stable identities make replay harmless.
More queues do not deduplicate.
Speed does not deduplicate.
variants.explanation: At-least-once transport should still produce one logical send.

variants.title: Read the promise
variants.context: An accepted intent is durable, no external send bypasses current policy, and retries create at most one logical channel delivery. Accepted means the platform owns the work, not that a provider or device delivered it.
variants.prompt: Policy was evaluated at enqueue time; the user opted out before the send. What must happen?
options: Policy is rechecked immediately before the external call; the send is suppressed and the reason recorded.
The send proceeds; policy was checked.
optionFeedback: An enqueue-time decision can become stale.
Stale policy must not reach a provider.
Opt-outs are immediate.

variants.title: Estimate the fan-out
variants.context: Baseline: 100 million intents per day, a 40× campaign peak toward a 50K per second target, 1.4 channel attempts per intent, 250 adapter calls per second per worker at 70% utilization.
variants.prompt: Peak intents are 46,280 per second with 1.4 channel attempts per intent. How many provider attempts per second before retries?

variants.title: Estimate the fan-out
variants.context: Baseline: 100 million intents per day, a 40× campaign peak toward a 50K per second target, 1.4 channel attempts per intent, 250 adapter calls per second per worker at 70% utilization.
variants.prompt: 64,792 attempts per second, 250 calls per second per worker, 70% target utilization. How many workers, rounded up?
variants.hint: Divide attempts by (calls per worker × utilization) and round up.

variants.title: Estimate the fan-out
variants.context: Baseline: 100 million intents per day, a 40× campaign peak toward a 50K per second target, 1.4 channel attempts per intent, 250 adapter calls per second per worker at 70% utilization.
variants.prompt: Demand is 80K attempts per second and dispatch capacity is 60K for a ten-minute burst. How many attempts accumulate?
variants.explanation: 20,000 × 600 = 12,000,000 attempts; oldest eligible message age, not depth, maps to the user-visible SLO.

variants.title: Apply the policy
variants.context: Critical messages may bypass marketing frequency caps but never consent rules, legal restrictions, destination validation, or provider quotas. An opt-out must stop queued marketing work before the next provider call. Only explicit policy authorizes channel fallback.
variants.prompt: A critical security alert hits a recipient’s marketing frequency cap. Send it?
options: Yes; critical may bypass marketing caps, but never consent, legal restrictions, destination validation, or provider quotas.
optionFeedback: Critical means bypassing product caps, not law or consent.
Caps are marketing controls.
Consent and legal rules always apply.
variants.hint: Which limits are product choices and which are not?
variants.explanation: Keep security and legally required messages in explicit policy classes.

variants.title: Apply the policy
variants.context: Critical messages may bypass marketing frequency caps but never consent rules, legal restrictions, destination validation, or provider quotas. An opt-out must stop queued marketing work before the next provider call. Only explicit policy authorizes channel fallback.
variants.prompt: Email to a user fails; SMS is available. Should the system fall back automatically?
options: Only if an explicit policy authorizes fallback; cost, consent, and experience differ by channel.
optionFeedback: Fallback is a policy decision, not a default.
Automatic fallback can violate consent or cost limits.
Explicit fallback is allowed.
variants.explanation: Only an explicit policy may authorize fallback.

variants.title: Apply the policy
variants.context: Critical messages may bypass marketing frequency caps but never consent rules, legal restrictions, destination validation, or provider quotas. An opt-out must stop queued marketing work before the next provider call. Only explicit policy authorizes channel fallback.
variants.prompt: A campaign with millions of queued sends is running when a user opts out. What must the platform do?
options: Stop the queued marketing work for that user before the next provider call.
Finish the campaign, then apply the opt-out.
optionFeedback: Opt-outs take effect before the next external call.
Delayed opt-outs are violations.
Any further send is a violation.
variants.hint: When must the opt-out be effective?
variants.explanation: Send-time policy checks make this possible.

variants.title: Track the state
variants.context: Provider acceptance, provider delivery, device receipt, and user engagement are distinct states. Callback events advance delivery state monotonically; a late accepted cannot overwrite delivered or permanently failed.
variants.prompt: The provider accepted the message. Did the user receive it?
options: Unknown; provider acceptance, provider delivery, device receipt, and engagement are distinct states.
Yes, if the device is online.
optionFeedback: Acceptance is the provider taking ownership.
Receipt is later evidence.
Online status is not receipt.
variants.hint: Which state does the evidence support?
variants.explanation: Do not promise 99.9% end-user delivery without defining eligible destinations.

variants.title: Track the state
variants.context: Provider acceptance, provider delivery, device receipt, and user engagement are distinct states. Callback events advance delivery state monotonically; a late accepted cannot overwrite delivered or permanently failed.
variants.prompt: A late accepted callback arrives after delivered was recorded. What happens?
options: It is ignored; state advances monotonically.
optionFeedback: Late events cannot overwrite later states.
Backward transitions corrupt status.
Nothing failed.
variants.explanation: Callback events advance delivery state monotonically.

variants.title: Track the state
variants.context: Provider acceptance, provider delivery, device receipt, and user engagement are distinct states. Callback events advance delivery state monotonically; a late accepted cannot overwrite delivered or permanently failed.
variants.prompt: Which states should the platform expose to callers?
options: accepted, scheduled, suppressed, dispatched, delivered, and failed, with the reason for suppression.
optionFeedback: Honest states let callers reason about outcomes.
One state hides suppression and failure.
Delivery alone hides everything before it.
variants.hint: What can the platform honestly report?
variants.explanation: Record the policy version and reason used for every suppression.

variants.title: Build the pipeline
variants.context: The pipeline: commit the intent and outbox event, expand audiences asynchronously, recheck policy immediately before the external call, call the provider with a stable attempt key, and advance state from callbacks monotonically.
variants.prompt: A product event triggers notifications. Put the pipeline in order.

items.text: Commit the intent and its outbox event, then acknowledge the caller with a notification_id.
Expand the audience asynchronously into recipient-channel deliveries with stable IDs.
Recheck consent, quiet hours, caps, and eligibility immediately before the external call.
Call the provider adapter with a stable attempt key inside the channel’s constrained lane.
Advance delivery state from callbacks monotonically.

variants.explanation: Slow personalization and providers stay off the acceptance path.

variants.title: Build the pipeline
variants.context: The pipeline: commit the intent and outbox event, expand audiences asynchronously, recheck policy immediately before the external call, call the provider with a stable attempt key, and advance state from callbacks monotonically.
variants.prompt: A provider returns an ambiguous result. Put the steps in order.

items.text: The intent was committed and acknowledged earlier.
The delivery had a stable channel_delivery_id.
Policy was rechecked before the call.
The retry reuses the same attempt key after the ambiguous result.
A deliberate failover creates a sequenced new attempt under the same logical delivery.

variants.hint: Same attempt key for retries; new sequenced attempt for failover.
variants.explanation: Retries reuse identity; failovers are explicit.

variants.title: Build the pipeline
variants.context: The pipeline: commit the intent and outbox event, expand audiences asynchronously, recheck policy immediately before the external call, call the provider with a stable attempt key, and advance state from callbacks monotonically.
variants.prompt: A campaign targets an audience of millions. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Accept and durably store one intent for the campaign.
Expand the audience asynchronously, not on the request path.
Recheck each recipient’s policy at send time.
Dispatch through per-provider and per-tenant constrained lanes.
Advance states from callbacks and track oldest eligible message age.

variants.hint: Audience expansion is asynchronous by design.
variants.explanation: Provider quotas, not CPU, are often the binding limit.
